doc.title: Buddy Tate interviewed by Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 3, 1995

chapter: Georgette's memories of the Basie band
title: Georgette Tate on her father; wanting to go to Hollywood
summary: Georgette praises her father, tells how at three she packed to go to the film shoot, and Tate recalls her birth.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: We’re back and we’re going to ask some more questions here and try to find out a few more colorful things with out guest, Buddy Tate. We would like to ask you, Georgette, if the two of you can kind of recall some experiences for us, perhaps like this?
I have many, many happy stories of my father.

When you’re raised with musicians, actors, singers, they are — I think that song best describes it that there’s no people like show people, and it’s true. He doesn’t like to hear this, I think they’re all rather shy like that. But as the children and as how we see it, they are different, they are special. And they are great, if I had all the money in the world I wouldn’t trade it for him as a father. He’s been my best friend, my advisor, he’s a very sensitive person and he’s a very wise man. I think as teenagers, you know how we can be when we’re young we feel like we know it all, but as I got older I really began to see how wise he was, if ever I have questions. But there’s so many funny stories. I remember when we were in California, I was about three years old, and he tells me this, I vaguely © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -11-

remember it, when he was making a movie. And I’ve always been a night owl, because he’d always get home at two or three and I’d always wait with him and we’d have breakfast early in the morning and I thought that was hot stuff. And he’d come home. And I heard something about movies, and I knew this, and I started to, my mother, he got up and I jumped up and I got my bag and I had my hat, and I was packing and trying to get ready and putting my shoes on the wrong feet, and Daddy always tells this story much funnier than I do, and my mother said something to the effect of, “why don’t you tell her that she’s not going.” And I knew, California, Hollywood, I knew that at three. And he said, “you tell her.” I remember this fair.

She says, “Mother, I see you’re not going. I’m going with Daddy.” She was about three years old. So she says, “I see you’re not going.” And she says, “but I’m going.” So I couldn’t take her though, at that time of morning, because we were making this picture, I don’t know if it was “Hellzapoppin” with Dorothy Dandridge. Anyway, but she wanted to go. She wanted to go everywhere I’d go. And I remember the night she was born, I wanted to see her to visit, and I was working, it was just about the time we were working at the Panther Room in Chicago and she called up and we’d have to go to work early in the afternoon. So one night I said, Basie says, “well go by there and talk to the lady.” So we went by there, and there she was, awake, at 3:00 in the morning. So and the lady says, “I could lose my job for this.” I said, “but I want to see my little girl” I says, “I haven’t seen her.” So she says, “okay, come on, cause Basie’s my favorite band.” So she let me see her and there she was, winking her eye. She used to wink her eye like this. I don’t know where she got that from. She used to be winking when I had her, she’d be winking and all. And people on the subway, I’d have her on the subway in New York and she’d be winking the eye and they’d break up the subway, cause people just couldn’t understand. They’d be holding her.
